new.headline: Race week has one job: arrive rested, confident and sharp on Sunday. Heavy legs and taper nerves are normal; the fitness is already in the bank from the 20-milers in Sep and Oct.

answers.question: Is it crazy to do one more 16-miler on Wednesday so I feel ready?
answers.answer: No, please do not add a 16-miler on Wednesday. Your last 20 was only eight days ago and the one before that was three weeks ago, so the long-run work is done and banked. A long run this week cannot add fitness; it can only drain the glycogen and freshness you need on Sunday. What you are feeling is classic taper legs plus pre-race nerves, and it almost always lifts in the last three or four days. Trust the work, keep the planned short runs honest and easy, and show up hungry on Sunday.

new.analysis:
## How last week went
You followed the taper plan cleanly: five runs, 34 miles, every session done at the planned distance, and the Wed workout hit marathon pace at 8:33 – 8:40/mi with an average heart rate of 147. The 12-mile long run averaged 10:00/mi at 146 bpm with a small drift, which is a healthy signal for Sunday. Nothing to fix here.

## Why the legs feel flat
When volume drops after a 46-mile week, the body starts repairing and refilling, and the first week often feels sluggish and heavy. The data backs that up: easy pace, easy heart rate and sleep are all steady, and pain stayed at 0 all week. That is a taper, not a fade.

## How to run Sunday
Your under-3:45 goal is 8:35/mi. Based on your 20-milers at 9:59/mi at 146 bpm and marathon-pace reps at 8:33 – 8:40/mi at 147, that pace is well within reach if you pace it right.

| Section | Pace plan |
| --- | --- |
| Miles 1 – 6 | 8:40 – 8:45/mi, let people pass you |
| Miles 7 – 20 | 8:30 – 8:35/mi, settle in |
| Miles 21 – 26.2 | 8:30/mi or whatever you have left |

Take fuel every 30 – 35 minutes from the start, and drink at every aid station after mile 3. Do not chase a time split in the first 10k; chase it in the last 10k.

## This week in one line
Short, easy, a touch of marathon pace to stay sharp, then a shakeout, then race.
